issues.legal_issue: Property allotted to a Hindu widow on partition under the Benares school is held as a widow’s estate and does not give her an absolute right to dispose of the corpus.
material_facts: The widow received properties on partition of her deceased husband’s estate.
The partition decree entitled her to income from the allotted properties but directed that she could not prejudice the reversioners by destroying the corpus.
issues.conclusion: The widow did not have an absolute interest in the properties allotted to her on partition; her interest stood on the same footing as property inherited from her husband.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Benares school of Mitakshara law, property allotted to a widow on partition was not her stridhan and stood on the same footing as property inherited from her husband. The Court relied on Bhugwandeen Doobey v. Myna Baee and followed Debi Mangal Prasad Singh v. Mahadeo Prasad Singh.

predicates.widow_partition_allotment_case: A dispute concerns property allotted to a Hindu widow on partition under the Benares school of Mitakshara law.
predicates.partition_decree_limited_use: The partition decree allowed the widow to receive income from the property while restricting her ability to dispose of its corpus to the prejudice of reversioners.
predicates.widow_received_property_from_deceased_hu: The widow received the disputed property as part of the division of her deceased husband’s estate.

issues.definition: When a widow receives property on partition and the decree or the nature of the allotment limits her use of its corpus, she holds a limited estate rather than absolute ownership.

issues.legal_issue: A Hindu widow may give her daughter a reasonable portion of her husband’s estate as marriage dowry after the marriage in fulfilment of an ante-nuptial promise, and the gift binds the reversioners.
material_facts: The widow promised during the settlement of her daughter’s marriage terms to give her four houses as marriage dowry.
The widow executed and registered a deed of gift for the houses about two years after the marriage.
The value of the houses was found not disproportionate or unreasonable in relation to the estate.
The courts found no reliable proof that a verbal gift was made at the marriage or that possession was delivered then.
issues.conclusion: The gift was valid and binding on the reversioners, notwithstanding that it was made after the marriage and no verbal gift at the marriage was proved.
issues.legal_principle: Hindu law treats a daughter’s marriage as a religious act conferring spiritual benefit on the father. A widow may alienate a reasonable portion of her husband’s estate for that purpose; an ante-nuptial promise may be fulfilled after the marriage, and it is not necessary to prove a sankalpa at the marriage. The Court reviewed decisions including Sardar Singh v. Kunj Behari Lal, Cossi Naut Bysack v. Hurroo Soondry Dossee, Kudutamma v. Narasimha Charyulu, Churaman Sahu v. Gopi Sahu, Sundararamayya v. Sitamma, Ram Sumran Prasad v. Gobind Das, and Pratap Kunwar v. Raj Bahadur Singh, and disapproved Ganga Bisheshar v. Pirthi Pal.

rule.if: widow_marriage_dowry_gift_case and antenuptial_promise_to_give_dowry and gift_fulfills_promise and gift_is_reasonable_portion and gift_formalities_completed

predicates.widow_marriage_dowry_gift_case: A reversioner challenges a Hindu widow’s transfer of her deceased husband’s property to her daughter as marriage dowry.
predicates.antenuptial_promise_to_give_dowry: The widow promised before the marriage to provide the daughter with property as marriage dowry.
predicates.gift_fulfills_promise: The widow made the transfer in fulfilment of that marriage-related promise, even though the transfer occurred after the marriage.
predicates.gift_is_reasonable_portion: The property transferred was a reasonable portion of the deceased husband’s estate in the circumstances.
predicates.gift_formalities_completed: The gift of immovable property was made by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses.

issues.definition: If a widow makes a formally effective and reasonable transfer to her daughter as marriage dowry in fulfilment of an ante-nuptial promise, the transfer binds the reversioners even when made after the marriage.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory requirements for making a gift of immovable property govern the gift’s legal effectiveness but do not extinguish a widow’s Hindu-law power to make a qualifying marriage-dowry gift after the marriage.
material_facts: The gift deed was executed and registered about two years after the marriage.
The gift fulfilled an ante-nuptial promise to provide the daughter with marriage dowry and involved a reasonable portion of the estate.
The deed was made by registered instrument in the prescribed manner.
issues.conclusion: The statutory form requirements did not prevent the widow from exercising her Hindu-law power to make the gift after the marriage; the gift was legally effective because the required form was observed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act requires a gift of immovable property to be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses. That provision governs the manner in which a gift becomes legally effective; it does not affect the Hindu-law power of a widow to make a qualifying gift of a reasonable portion of her husband’s estate as marriage dowry.

predicates.widow_hindu_law_gift_case: A widow makes a transfer that is claimed to be within her Hindu-law power to dispose of property for a daughter’s marriage.
predicates.qualifying_marriage_dowry_gift: The transfer is a reasonable marriage-dowry gift to the daughter made in fulfilment of a marriage-related promise.
predicates.statutory_gift_form_observed: The immovable-property gift was effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses.

issues.definition: When a widow makes a qualifying marriage-dowry gift and observes the required form for transferring immovable property, those form requirements do not defeat her underlying Hindu-law power to make the gift.
